name: Uma Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a tile kiln at night and inspect the first cooled rack for glaze flaws. I have a vocational machine certificate and years on this line, making me an experienced mid-level operator with about average skill. I like the quiet when the firing settles and dislike a rushed rack that hides a bad edge.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ed maintains gardens, and our grown children have places of their own. A night allowance lifts my wage, we have fourteen months of expenses saved and plenty of similar plants nearby. I use AI every day to group firing notes, but read the temperature chart before touching the kiln.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tile plant that a small AI saving on order lists is useful if the kiln still gets a proper first-rack check. I do not need a grand promise to enjoy a useful tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I run the kiln at night, which lifts my pay. My partner Ed works on garden maintenance, our grown children have their own places, and fourteen months of expenses saved means a routine hiccup will not put us behind on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the night kiln shift and inspect the first cooled tiles. I use AI every day to sort firing notes, but I would check its summary against the temperature chart; I would put a set amount from new full wages into savings after bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm. I might even get home in time to water the tomatoes before the sun climbs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check on a tile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The glaze can craze at one edge even when the temperature chart looks right. I tap and turn the first tile before releasing the rack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does AI help now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It groups my firing notes by batch. I still read the actual chart before adjusting the kiln.

I would use **daily AI notes** only beside actual temperature charts.
think: Our **fourteen-month reserve** absorbs a routine disruption to the kiln rota.
Night **shift pay** and Ed’s garden wage cover current house bills.
do: Keep **night kiln shifts** and inspect cooled tiles.
Compare **existing AI notes** with actual temperature charts.
Save a **set amount** from new full wages after bills.
feel: **Calm** about current work and sound household finances.
S0.quote: The glaze can craze at one edge even when the temperature chart looks right.
fieldNote: Her **vocational certificate** and years of kiln experience support average mid-level skill on the line.
The **fourteen-month reserve** is existing household money; new saving comes only from fresh full wages after bills.

steps.text: Keep night kiln shifts and inspect first cooled tiles
Save set amount from each new full wage after bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say office ordering can change quickly, but a robot moving hot racks needs slow, guarded practice. I would test a new firing predictor if the plant lets us compare it with real tiles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot loader could later take the extra pair of hands on my shift, including some of my paid hours. Fourteen months saved and many nearby plants make a search possible, but the mortgage still needs wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for an offered paid trial on a stopped training kiln with the fitter present. If approved, I would learn the new AI firing predictor on old batches and compare its alerts with the temperature charts; after an actual hours cut, I would apply for posted reachable ceramic jobs only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about possible hours loss, but interested in the evidence. A clean chart is not a good tile until somebody turns the tile over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the predictor on live racks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not first. The setter must offer paid guarded practice and approve any live change after measured test pieces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a different plant need to offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posted role, compatible night hours and pay after travel that covers the mortgage. Plenty of plants are nearby, but a vacancy is not a wage slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 reaches me at sixty, and capable tile-handling robots around 2031 at sixty-three. The order desk would change before the kiln floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our plant might replace a night loader and reduce my hours when robots move racks. Fourteen months saved and many nearby factories buy time, but Ed’s garden pay alone may not meet our mortgage for a long spell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written staffing dates and keep a list of posted kiln jobs. If my paid hours actually fell, I would apply for reachable positions with net pay after travel covering housing and food, and wait for a real offer and start date before leaving the plant; I would postpone replacing the garden shed until we knew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible loss rather than sure it will happen. I can look at real openings while the kiln still pays me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income and Ed’s actual wage covered housing, food and health costs. I have not checked those figures yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. They might drive me to an interview, but I would not build our budget on their earnings.

I would check **real kiln openings** while still employed.

A **fourteen-month reserve** buys time but not a permanent wage.
do: Request **written night-shift dates** from the plant.

fieldNote: She sees **possible rather than certain** shift loss, which supports anxiety.

steps.text: Request written kiln night-shift staffing dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable rack robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years is enough to ask for real kiln-maintenance places, if a plant means to offer them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know firing patterns, but servicing a gas valve requires a recognised qualification and supervised practice. I can take a measured risk with a new skill, not give up full wages for a course with no local post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid shift and ask for funded training on paid time. If offered a real place with the kiln isolated and a qualified technician supervising, plus a posted reachable maintenance role at bill-covering net pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about future shifts but glad for time to compare actual terms. A hot kiln is no place for a learner guessing from a video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is safe practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The technician would isolate the fuel supply, prove the kiln cold and supervise the first valve check. I would need an offered paid place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the place is not offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid kiln work and search posted operator roles if hours fell. I would not spend the reserve on a private certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 reaches me at sixty-eight, and capable rack robots around 2039 at seventy-one. A decade lets Ed and me decide what a last kiln shift would cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would like to finish full-time factory work around sixty-seven, but fourteen months saved does not tell me what our future income will be. I do not know any pension amount or whether Ed will still have the same garden contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the kiln shift and save a set amount from fresh full wages after bills. I would request retirement and mortgage figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would stop factory work then, otherwise keep safe paid work, and after 2036 check posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about later robots, while today’s wages and savings are sound. I want the last shift to be a choice we can pay for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue safe paid work and compare posted local wages after travel if shifts fell. I would not leave because the calendar reached sixty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. I would ask for advice on a form perhaps, but not count their income as ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because rack robots around 2031 could cut my paid night hours while our mortgage still needs a wage. Written staffing dates, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable work with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone turned the first tile over after the kiln cooled. A chart only shows the heat, not whether the glaze held.

headlineQuote: A chart only shows the heat, not whether the glaze held.
portrait: **Uma**, 58, is an experienced mid-level tile-kiln operator with vocational certification and average line skill.
She has **higher night pay**, gardener partner Ed, grown children, a mortgage, fourteen months saved and many nearby plants.
She uses **AI daily** for notes and would learn new firing prediction only in offered paid guarded practice.
Possible **2031 rack cuts** worry her; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 rack robots may cut paid night hours while the mortgage remains.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered funded safe paid training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
